extracted.intended_audience: EPA regulators, state environmental agencies, and legal counsel for electric utilities/cooperatives
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/administrative-comment arguing the EPA Proposed Rule under CAA §111(d) is unlawful because it (1) exceeds EPA’s guidance-only authority, (2) conflicts with existing implementing regulations, and (3) fails to permit states to consider remaining useful life and other source-specific factors when setting standards for particular sources. Intended for the notice-and-comment record.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA guideline documents are informational only (40 C.F.R. §60.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline documents under 40 C.F.R. §60.22 are nonbinding “guideline document[s]” “containing information pertinent to control of the designated pollutant from designated facilities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation repeatedly uses the words “guidance” and “information,” and specifies the purely informational purposes of guideline documents: (1) information concerning endangerment; (2) description of emission reduction systems adequately demonstrated; (3) degree of emission reduction achievable with each system and costs/environmental effects; (4) incremental time periods for design/installation/startup; (5) an emission guideline reflecting application of the best system of emission reduction (considering cost) adequately demonstrated and time to achieve equivalent stringency, with subcategorization where appropriate; and (6) other available information the Administrator determines useful. Because these are informational, EPA may not issue guideline documents that in practice contain binding statewide emission reduction goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA may not adopt a rule conflicting with its existing regulations without rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may change longstanding regulations only through ordinary notice-and-comment rulemaking; it may not propose a rule that conflicts with existing rules and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting a rule that conflicts with prior regulations without explanation is arbitrary and capricious (citing Brand X/unexplained inconsistency). If EPA wishes to depart from past rules, it must revise underlying rules via proper rulemaking and explain the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards must be applicable to individual sources under §111(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d) anticipates States will be “applying a standard of performance to any particular source,” indicating standards are to be applied with particularity to specific units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language and structure show two expectations: (1) States will look with particularity at specific units applying standards of performance; and (2) EPA’s guidelines must allow States to make prudential assessments about remaining useful life and other source-specific factors when determining the extent to which to apply standards to each unit. The focus of standard-setting must therefore be whether the unit itself can meet the prescribed standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "new source" and "existing source" implies source-specific application
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(a)(2) defines “new source” as any stationary source whose construction/modification commences after publication of regulations prescribing a standard applicable to such source; “existing source” is any stationary source other than a new source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions refer to “any stationary source” (i.e., single identifiable sources), indicating congressional intent that standards apply to individual sources rather than broad categories without source-specific consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: States must be permitted to consider "remaining useful life" when applying standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1977 Amendments added language requiring that regulations “shall permit the State in applying a standard of performance to any particular source … to take into consideration, among other factors, the remaining useful life of the existing source to which such standard applies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history (House and Conference Reports) confirms Congress intended standards for existing sources to take into account remaining useful life; this was viewed as an essential state power. EPA must meaningfully allow states to consider remaining useful life rather than relying on generic or illusory flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 40 C.F.R. §60.24(f) factors allowing less stringent standards or longer schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: 40 C.F.R. §60.24(f) authorizes States (unless otherwise specified) to provide for less stringent emissions standards or longer compliance schedules provided the State demonstrates, with respect to each facility (or class): (1) unreasonable cost of control resulting from plant age, location, or basic process design; (2) physical impossibility of installing necessary control equipment; or (3) other factors specific to the facility (or class) that make a less stringent standard or final compliance time significantly more reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulation was promulgated in 1975 as a case‑by‑case exception mechanism and does not mention “remaining useful life.” It permits case-specific relief for cost/physical/legal impediments, but, by itself, does not satisfy the statutory requirement added in 1977 that States be permitted to consider remaining useful life among other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Standard of performance" statutory definition constrains EPA and States (42 U.S.C. §111(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1977 CAA Amendments define “standard of performance” for categories and for particular sources: (A) for fossil fuel fired category—establishing allowable emission limitations and requiring percentage reduction from uncontrolled fuel; (B) for other categories—similar limitations; (C) for a particular source— a standard the State (or Administrator in limited circumstances) determines applicable to that source which reflects the degree of emission reduction achievable through BSER (considering cost, nonair health/environmental impacts, and energy requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For categories (A/B) standard must reflect degree of emission limitation achievable through best technological system of continuous emission reduction (taking into account cost, nonair impacts, energy). For particular sources, the standard must reflect achievable degree of reduction via BSER considering the same factors; fuel cleaning prior to combustion may be credited per regulations. This framework requires source-appropriate assessments and cost/impact considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress distinguished new vs existing sources to prevent treating existing units as new
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress created two distinct classes—new and existing sources—with different standards, anticipating that some existing units cannot meet aggressive goals without curtailment or shutdown, and prescribing procedures (allowing state adjustment) instead of forcing closures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where improvements are infeasible, statute contemplates relaxation of the standard rather than treating existing sources like new sources; permitting states to consider remaining useful life avoids premature shutdown and stranded investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA cannot use state-wide binding targets that effectively strip states' authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A target premised on maximum emission reductions from all units (a binding state-wide target) can impermissibly strip States of their statutory authority to develop standards that account for the remaining useful life of specific facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a plan gives some flexibility about how reductions are achieved, a binding statewide target that presumes maximum reductions from all units forces particular facilities to bear reductions (or be retired) and makes purported state flexibility illusory because compliance would require shuttering or transferring burdens to other facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must provide meaningful regulatory text/mechanism to allow consideration of remaining useful life
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble statements that flexibility exists in plan development are insufficient; EPA must include provisions in regulatory text that permit States to account for remaining useful life and other source-specific factors in a meaningful way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency’s reliance on general plan flexibility and invitations for comment does not satisfy the statutory requirement. 40 C.F.R. §60.24(f) was not intended to and does not by itself implement the 1977 remaining useful life requirement. EPA should allow different glide paths, endpoint dates, or facility-specific adjustments (with appropriate compensating emission reductions) so states can avoid premature retirements and stranded investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative federalism and local expertise requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of cooperative federalism requires EPA to respect State prerogatives and local knowledge when implementing BSER across the national electricity generation sector; EPA cannot efficiently make site‑by‑site judgments from Washington.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation must recognize that no central agency can attain the local knowledge necessary for prudent judgments about effectiveness and feasibility of BSER at individual units; states must be able to tailor standards to fit their fleets of existing sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to avoid premature retirements and stranded investments when setting standards/timing
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposed standards and compliance timing would force retirement decades before a unit’s remaining useful life (e.g., units undergoing recent large capital investments based on assumed operation for ≥20 years), EPA must allow adjustments so those investments are not stranded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Big Stone (South Dakota) installing a $400M scrubber assumed 20-year life; Laramie River Station units with $250M per unit investments based on 20-year assumptions. EPA’s rule must permit different glide paths or timing so states with few affected EGUs can preserve operation at economically viable production levels throughout remaining useful life.
